To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the air-blood barrier is permeable to pulmonary surfactants used as electron-opaque tracers.

the air-blood barrier is not impermeable to surfactant, that the barrier is permeable to surfactants in both directions, and that the barrier is more permeable to surfactive lipids than to the proteins of surfactant.

pulmonary surfactant, used as an electron opaque tracer, was transported by quants from the alveoli through type I alvesolar cells to the interstitial space and then to the lymphatic and blood vessels by plasmalemml vesicles, and to a lesser degree, by open channels formed by fusion of the plasmalemma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and function of the alveolus, the functional unit of the lung.
a study of the ultrastructure of the lung and its relationship to the pathophysiology of the disease.
the transport of pulmonary surfactants from the alveoli to the blood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium are not barriers to surfactant and that the basement membrane is a barrier.

surfactant is normally transported through the air-blood interface by the following routes: (1) from alveolar surface to basement membrane by vesicles and open membrane-lined channels; (2) from basement membrane across endothelial cells to blood by vesicles; (3) from basement membrane to alveolar macrophages by pinocytosis and phagocytosis.
the alveolar capillary barrier is not an impenetrable barrier to pulmonary surfatant, but that the barrier is highly selective in that it allows only certain molecules to pass through.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the alveolar capillary barrier was not a barrier to surfactant.

the air-blood barrier is a permeable membrane which allows the transport of water, electrolytes, and proteins from blood to alveoli and of pulmonary surfactants from alveoli to the lymphatic and vascular systems.
surfactant is transported from the alveolus to the lymphatic by a process of pinocytosis, which is the most important mechanism for removal of surfactants from the alveoli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the alveolar epithelium is a barrier to surfactant movement, and this barrier is a dynamic structure that is involved in the transport of surfactant.
pulmonary surfactant is a very dynamic substance and its turnover and transport through the air-blood interface of the alveolus are important in maintaining normal lung function.
pulmonary surfactant is not only a surface-active material that reduces surface tension in the airways, but also that it has a number of other important roles in the lung.
